utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom and to those who are listening to these hearings. Due to technical problems again like last week, we had a later start, but I hope everybody's in agreement that we should use the time and start even without proper working LiveNote. Witness, welcome again to the courtroom. May I remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir has some more questions for you. Mr. Tolimir, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May the Lord bless this house, and may the divine providence bring justice, not according to my wishes but according to God's will. I would like to greet everyone in and around the courtroom, and I would like to greet the witness. Let us conclude this exercise in keeping with God's will.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last time we left off while discussing your arrival and stay with UNPROFOR. During examination-in-chief, it was said that you worked in many a country. However, no clear distinction was made whether you served there as a peacekeeper or in some other capacity. Could you please share with us what countries you were in, and I believe you addressed that in the Popovic case, and what was your position there.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My posting to Sarajevo in 1995 was my last real military posting, and in 1996 I joined the NGO the Halo Trust, which is a de-mining charity, and since April 1996, I've been working for the Halo Trust. So time that I've spent in Mozambique, the Caucasus, Afghanistan, Kosovo again briefly, Cambodia, Sri Lanka, Somaliland, have all been as part of a de-mining programme and in no way connected to peacekeeping and not on a UN contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Popovic case you said that you were in Afghanistan, Mozambique, Chechnya, Kosovo, Cambodia, South Lebanon, et cetera. Am I correct or have I misinterpreted something?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're absolutely correct. South Lebanon I was actually detached briefly from Halo, and I was with ICJ, who were looking at abuses of international law and they wanted somebody who had some understanding of weapons and weapon systems. So I accompanied them in that role.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain in more detail in what capacity you worked for the ICJ. What was your position? Who were you employed by, and anything else you might share with us.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. I was literally just attached to them. So I had no contract with ICJ. I wasn't paid by ICJ. They wanted somebody who could offer opinions on certain things, recognise ammunition and the like. My boss in Halo saw it as a useful opportunity for me to go to South Lebanon, and while I was there have a look at the cluster ammunition and mines problem at the same time. So I did two trips; one lasted three weeks, and the other maybe four weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the ICJ perhaps require an expert with your or similar background, and did they request Halo to provide one; or did you get in touch with the ICJ by some other means or through some other channels, because I don't believe you acted in an expert capacity on that occasion? What was exactly your role?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. ICJ contacted Halo first, so that's -- that's where the -- the invitation came from. They were looking for someone particularly who -- who had experience of bombing and the like, use of -- use of airpower, and I didn't fit that role particularly, so again I was more useful to them and after many years with Halo Trust where a lot of time is dealing with unexploded ammunition, so seeing bits and pieces on the ground and commenting on that. In reality, it was a fairly small role. What I did get to do was sit in during pretty much all the other interviews that ICJ conducted with people who had been displaced by the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you appointed by a state or a party in a proceedings before that court, or were you appointed by the court itself?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's ICJ -- we may be talking about different things. It wasn't a -- not a court. I'm just trying to remember what it actually stood for now. To be honest, it's escaped my mind what it does stand for, but it wasn't the -- not the Court of Justice. It was a -- again, it's a nongovernmental body that -- slightly similar to Amnesty International. So they work with Amnesty, but aren't Amnesty, looking at abuses of international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to greet everyone in the courtroom. For the transcript, I would just like to ask the interpreters not to translate ICJ as the International Court of Justice, which they have mistakenly have been doing, hence Mr. Tolimir's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you clarify where you find it? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Maybe I can help move things along a little bit. It may be that the ICJ to which the witness is referring is the International Commission of Jurists. I just throw that out there and see if that helps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand, and I think the witness said it is not the International Court of Justice. Therefore the transcript is, in my understanding, quite clear. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise to the witness and everyone else, because he cleared it up only of after a number of questions, whereas before that we received interpretation to the effect that it was the International Court of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since you worked for number of NGOs, such as the de-mining trust as well as the International Commission of Jurists, did you work for any other NGO in the countries you visited?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I -- as I said before, my entire time from 1996 has been with Halo Trust, and even while I was attached to the -- to ICJ, that was still being paid for by Halo Trust, and it was a very brief attachment. The rest of my time I've had one single employer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Halo Trust as an NGO, was it registered in the countries you visited, or is it registered in the UK, the United States, or any other country for that matter?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's registered in both Britain and the United States, and then in every country that we go to, it's one of the very first steps we have to do is to get registration done with the national government or whichever happens to be the line ministry that deals with either NGOs in general or with de-mining in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Afghanistan, Mozambique, Chechnya, Kosovo, Sri Lanka, Lebanon, were the conflicts in all these countries which you visited -- did these conflicts ensue before you visited Bosnia or following your trip to Bosnia, and to what extent have you been successful in actually carrying out de-mining in those countries?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a country like Afghanistan, the conflict has obviously started before our time in Bosnia and continues until today, and it does vary from country to country. In Chechnya, for instance, I was there between 1997 and the very end of 1999. So I missed the first war but was there for the start of the second. De-mining's a slow progress -- is a slow process. I think in terms of -- of progress itself, our biggest success is probably Northern Mozambique where we've, to all intents and purposes, finished. In other countries, some other countries the end is in sight, and in places like Afghanistan, Cambodia, Angola, there's still a long way to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the structure of the UN peacekeeping forces in these countries? Was it similar to the structure UNPROFOR had in Bosnia in terms of its position vis-a-vis the parties included in such conflicts?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, very different, and in some places absolutely no UN presence at all. So in the Caucasus, for instance, no UN presence. In Afghanistan, the first time I went in 1998, again the UN were largely based out of Pakistan at that stage and weren't playing any military peacekeeping role. The international role, the UN role in Afghanistan now isn't military. That's under a completely different chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the countries we enumerated, were you there whilst the conflicts were still in progress or only after they ceased? I believe that was the gist of my previous question.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies for a rather lengthy, incorrect answer. Chechnya, I was there definitely as the second war started and witnessed a fair bit of that. Afghanistan, the conflict has been ongoing. I've based there for most of the last three years with, in the parts of the country where we were, relatively low-intensity conflict going on around us. Sri Lanka, when I was there the conflict was at some remove, maybe 50 kilometres from where we were based. And in the other countries, the conflict tended to be finished when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now move on to your statement, which we used last time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 1D278.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It is your statement of the 20th -- 28th December 1996, given to representatives of this Tribunal. We can see it in English now. Thank you. In the Popovic case you said that -- it is page 16266, lines 10 to 12, you said that you were based at Bosnia command headquarters where you worked for General Smith as a liaison officer. I quote: "My principal role was to liaise with the Serb side." Is this correct, and please explain in more detail how you went about that.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, and I took over from Milos Stankovic, or Mike Stanley, who had a close working relationship, I would say, with the Serb side. It involved talking to -- talking to specific individuals, and a lot of it involved carrying messages or preparing ground for people higher up the chain of command in HQ UNPROFOR. So very often what we were doing was trying to set up a meeting for either General Smith or on occasion we were used to set up meetings for the UN Civil Affairs side as the fact that we had physical connections on the ground with individuals meant that we were better placed to do that than people in the civil affairs side. The role for me became quite difficult following the -- the air-strikes in late May, I believe it was, and from that period onwards communication, particularly as far as Pale, became considerably more difficult than before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your role only to liaise with the Serb side, or did you establish contact with the other parties to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fairly shortly after I arrived, a second liaison officer was brought in, Captain Emma Bliss, and her primary role was dealing with the other side. I did accompany General Smith. I can remember one occasion when I accompanied him to see Minister Muratovic. We saw Prime Minister Izetbegovic once, and I do remember going across to Tuzla with Colonel Coiffet, again talking to representatives of the Bosnian side in Tuzla. But primarily General Smith tried to keep us separated, so Emma dealt with one side and I dealt with the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your position or role in those contacts between Mr. Smith and Muratovic and Izetbegovic? Did you act as interpreter or liaison officer? What was precisely your role?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: More liaison officer. My language simply wasn't good enough to deal with proper interpretation at a meeting of that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The contacts you had with General Smith and Mr. Muratovic and Izetbegovic, did they have to do with the events in Zepa and Srebrenica in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember exactly when and which ones I participated in. I -- I know that between Srebrenica and Zepa, so around 17th, 19th of July, Muratovic was in touch with General Smith's office trying to establish some way of evacuating the civilian population, making sure they left safely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the same topic discussed in conversations with President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't remember what we discussed, but I'm fairly sure that the chronology was such that Zepa-Srebrenica was not discussed at the meeting that I attended with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D60 in e-court. It is a letter by Alija Izetbegovic, dated the 18th of July, 1995, sent to General Delic. It mentions a meeting with General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Perhaps we can use this to jog your memory, and then I would like to ask you whether this was actually on the agenda. It is a short letter. In item 1 it says: "I have just been talking to General Smith. Perhaps I could have women, children and the elderly from Zepa evacuated by UNPROFOR. Would you accept this?" It was Izetbegovic addressing General Delic. In item 2: "Perhaps in this case we could insert a brigade ... of soldiers to Zepa, across the forest path and thus continue the combat ... these men from Zepa say that they could find between 500 and 1.000 volunteers ... "3. Groups should also be inserted into Gorazde ... "4. An evacuation plan for the population of Zepa has been made here in case items 1 and 2 above fail. I am sending it to you. I am waiting for your answers ..." It seems that Alija Izetbegovic is referring to a meeting with General Smith whereby he discussed the evacuation of women, children and the elderly on the 17th, as you mentioned yourself. Do you recall such a conversation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, I'm -- I'm confident that the meeting which I attended with Izetbegovic was -- was not during this particular period. So this is perhaps one that somebody else attended with General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you mentioned the 17th or the 18th. That is why I showed you the letter of the 18th. I thought that might be the same case, the same issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember those -- those dates that we were in discussion with -- with Muratovic, but as I said, the meeting that we had with -- with Izetbegovic, the one that I attended I'm completely confident didn't deal with these issues and would have been at a different period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to remind you. And now I'm going to ask you this: Your job as a liaison officer, did it also include gathering information about problems which you evidenced as a liaison officer during contacts that you attended in your capacity as liaison officer for General Smith? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean was part of the job to be told problems with the people we liaised with and pass those back to General Smith's headquarters, yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you went to Zepa, did you compile information about the situation in Zepa? Did you have contacts there between General Smith and General Mladic, and did you brief him about the situation in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our trip to Zepa came at, certainly for me, very short notice, and I think I referred to it in the notes before. I literally got woken up at half past midnight and was told we were leaving at 4.30 that morning. So as far as preparation for that trip itself, there was virtually none. However, as we've mentioned previously, there was a build-up of information coming. I remember it being from Minister Muratovic rather than from Izetbegovic, discussing what -- what to do with the civilian population, but I certainly wasn't in my role driving that process. I was not tasked to collect information on what was happening with Zepa, build up a document and brief the general on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me -- actually, tell the Trial Chamber, not me, what did Muratovic ask of General Smith, as you were present at that meeting and General Smith did go to Zepa. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall, he actually wanted to meet, himself, with General Smith, and that was -- the debate then ensued as to where the meeting would take place. I think General Mladic suggested it happened on territory controlled by VRS, and I think Minister Muratovic said he would only accept something in neutral ground, for instance, the airport, which was rejected. We went with General Smith, and, I think, yes, the idea was then that General Smith would talk with Mladic to see what message he could get for -- on behalf of Muratovic. We got as far as Lukavica barracks and General Mladic then passed a message to say he personally could not come but we dealt through Colonel Indic. And the message that we got, I believe, was that the only conditions that General Mladic would consider was unconditional surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember any other requests that Muratovic asked of UNPROFOR in relation to Zepa as you attended those meetings? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right now I don't, no. I'm aware that Muratovic continued to deal with General Smith whilst I was on the ground in Zepa, but I wasn't party to any of those subsequent discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it would be easier for you to remember what I'm going to ask you about, we're going to go by dates. On page 2 of your statement, if you can turn to page 2, please, paragraph 3, which has two lines only.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1D278. Can we please show that so that the witness could see it. Page 2, please. Thank you. We can see it in English. We can also see it in the Serbian. Page 2, paragraph 3, please, on page 2, lines 1 and 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We're looking at that paragraph 3, it's short, and it says: "One of the tasks I carried out was when I attended the evacuation of DutchBat with Brigadier General Nicolai on the 19th of July, 1995. I met and had a good talk to General Mladic that day." My question is: What was the task you and General Nicolai had in Srebrenica on the 19th, as you said, and at that time, did you sign any kind of agreement with General Mladic or any kind of document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the day when the Dutch troops were leaving Srebrenica, and as General Nicolai was himself a Dutch officer, he was going down in person to witness that event. And again I was notified at short notice to accompany General Nicolai for basic interpreting and smoothing the route, getting through check-points on the way. I don't remember us signing anything. I remember we met Mladic on the road. He was briefing people. We then went down to Bratunac, had a brief meal in Bratunac and then saw the troops leaving and walked through Srebrenica briefly. That's my recollections of that particular day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on the 19th of July, 1995, was an evacuation of the DutchBat carried out from Srebrenica, and was it conducted pursuant to some kind of agreement between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Dutch Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. I think there had been quite a bit of backwardsing and forwardsing amongst the more senior staff. I think -- I may be wrong is this, but I think at that period General Smith himself might have gone across to Belgrade as part of the discussions as to how this was going to proceed, how the evacuation would take place. So definitely it wasn't an ad hoc event. It had been talked about and planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us how this ended, and how did you in the UNPROFOR evaluate that activity of moving the DutchBat out of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a purely logistical point of view, it appeared to run fairly smoothly. The troops were ready, permissions were granted, and I remember them driving off across the bridge without any particular difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to move to a different event that happened immediately afterwards, and you said: "After the fall of Srebrenica in July, I was sent to Tuzla." This is the fourth paragraph, immediately after the third one on this page 2. You can see it. You can read it yourself. I will be putting questions to you from this paragraph. You said that there was great disorder in UNPROFOR in Tuzla and that Colonel Coiffet was trying to sort the situation out and that, amongst other things, you also spoke to some refugees. And then in the last sentence you say: "... there were only a few men who with a few old men had -- a few women who with a few old men had made it out to Tuzla from Srebrenica." Can you tell us a little bit more about this disorder in UNPROFOR and what exactly was the nature of these problems that you were supposed to resolve? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you'll find that it'd be a classic, certainly from my view, conflict on military organisation versus civilian organisation, and we were slightly taken aback on arriving in Tuzla to find that there wasn't a 24-hour manned Operations Room to deal with this particular crisis, which in a military situation, of course, there would have been. So that was -- that was set up. I think the scale of everything had slightly caught people off guard, not quite expecting such a rush, not prepared for it in Srebrenica. So again, it was to get people who could try and direct that, try and organise it slightly better, and also pass a message back to General Smith's headquarters to let him know -- people he knew could pass a message back and say this is what we're seeing on the ground. My recollection of the people is as per my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question for the witness, actually. Witness, on page 14 of the transcript, when Defence asked you how do you assess the departure of the DutchBat from Srebrenica, you answered that from a logistical, strictly logistical point of view, the operations went well, and Defence did not proceed that line of questioning and ask you whether there were any other points of view for you to assess that operation. So you have told us about the strictly logistical point of view, but which other points of view or point of views could you assess it on and did you not specify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was certainly a political point of view, and perhaps a military point of view, and it was a very depressing event essentially seeing UNPROFOR troops leaving Srebrenica. So, yes, they left without difficulty, but -- I don't know what -- what other angle you're looking on that when they left, which is a disappointment which I can say from a personal feeling. Does that answer your question sufficiently, or are you looking for something else particular?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like you to go a little more in-depth. Certainly when you're talking about logistical point of views, you're setting it separate from other points of views. Now, you've referred to some. You're talking about your personal point of view and you speak of disappointment, but what other angles were there? That's what I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By that particular date the civilian population of Srebrenica had largely left, so what we were witnessing was very much the aftermath of it. So those were the last UNPROFOR troops leaving town. There, outside the Dutch Battalion building, I remember seeing a great deal of debris on the ground that had been left behind by the civilian population of Srebrenica before they left the -- left the enclave. So there was that, but I didn't see any of the civilian population actually leaving. From a political point of view, as I've said, there were higher-level meetings conducted prior to this date. I personally didn't attend those higher-level meetings, but my understanding is that details were agreed as to how this evacuation would take place, and as far as I could tell, the evacuation or withdrawal of the Dutch troops took place in accordance with that agreement. There didn't seem to be any conflict at all between General Nicolai or General Mladic as to the logistics, for want of another word, how it was conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much. I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us if there were any problems with the civilian population that left Zepa to go to Tuzla, as you said earlier in this paragraph, and what were these problems?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clarify, that left Zepa or left Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. I said Zepa, but I should have said Srebrenica, because this was after the fall of Srebrenica. So those who left Srebrenica. Thank you. And did this include members of the UNHCR and members of other civilian organisations, as well as yourself?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: With regards to problems concerning the civilian population, it was -- as we would expect, they were fairly traumatised, I would have said, completely exhausted, having left their homes no doubt in some degree of peril, been transported to Srebrenica -- sorry, to Kladanj and then on to Tuzla. They had with them only what they could carry. They were concerned about the male members of their families who were not with them. And at that stage, UNHCR, the UN in general, had not yet come forward with sufficient assets in terms of food, shelter, whatever, for these people. That all took some time to gear up. With regards to who was involved, UNHCR would have been the -- the lead agency, but also working with the Bosnian government. ICRC were involved, as were, I believe, a number of other non-governmental organisations, though I couldn't give you any specific names of who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were monitoring the problem and your sector in Tuzla was doing so, did your command and General Smith receive a report about how many refugees left Srebrenica and how many of them were registered once they arrived in Tuzla by those who were doing the registering? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did the UNPROFOR have any kind of figure that they got from the UNHCR and other civilian organs or the international organisations that were registering these refugees? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Popovic case we were shown a document from UN Civil Affairs which talked about numbers, number of people who had perhaps been killed leaving. So I'm aware that that sort of document was going backwards and forwards between Tuzla and Sarajevo, but again the specifics of who saw what, I'm not in a position to tell you or tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I wasn't asking you about men but women, the elderly, and children once they were transported out. So how many of those women, the elderly, and children that were transported reached Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm simply -- I'm simply not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. We will ask those who did that together with you, those who were in charge of that particular matter. I want to ask you this: You said on the last line that only a few women with a few old men had made it out to Tuzla from Srebrenica. Did they reach Tuzla on their own or were they transported from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that they were transported from Srebrenica as far as Kladanj and then from Kladanj separately on to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please tell us when you were in Srebrenica, when you were in Tuzla, and later when you were in Zepa, what capacity were you there in since General Smith at the time was away. He was absent from Tuzla and absent from Bosnia. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: We quite often use the expression as being somebody's eyes and ears on the ground, so part of it would have been that. Eyes and ears for headquarters to see what was happening and make sure a fairly accurate, as far as possible, and timely report was sent back to the headquarters that could be forwarded to General Smith while he was away if that was deemed necessary. And again, that wasn't my call as to what was forwarded to General Smith whilst on leave. And indeed, even from Zepa we were reporting on the JCO net which then got passed on to Colonel Baxter, and he would then decide what was passed on to General Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And since you said earlier that you were the eyes and the ears, does that mean that someone else was also doing that job for your command, and were you compiling information there in some other way except the audio and visual way? So information in another way from what you were able to see and hear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking the question of me specifically, or was HQ UNPROFOR collecting additional sources of information? Me, personally, I was recording what I saw, talking to people, what they reported back to me. At HQ level, obviously there was more than just me. There were the JCOs. There were reports coming from the civilian side. That would all have been compiled in the operations cell or somewhere within the HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I meant you, since you had said you were the eyes and the ears, and I thought that was your JCO team that was in that capacity doing that, and you can tell me if I'm correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was, again, their primary role, but Coiffet and I went looking at it. We may have talked to different people or may have seen a slightly different aspect of it, but again, what we were doing was reporting back what we saw and heard. So possibly an overlap of roles, but nothing particular different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These JCO teams, were they in Srebrenica, in Zepa? And as far as I know, these were special units of the British Army or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were in -- JCOs were made up of SAS troops, and they were weren't necessarily permanently based in one place. So to the best of my knowledge, in Zepa the JCOs deployed at the same time as I did, and we went out together. I am aware that there were teams in Srebrenica at the time of -- of the evacuation, at the time of the fighting around DutchBat, but personally, I had nothing to do with the deployment of them, and I wouldn't necessarily have known all the deployments of them. That was, again, somebody else's command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And now that you are mentioning another chain of command, are they subordinated to the British Armed Forces and officers, or are they subordinated to UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, ultimately they would have been reporting to HQ UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And were they personally under the command of General Smith or were they subordinated to superiors within UNPROFOR who were in charge that area or region? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that it would have been -- all troops in Bosnia would have been directed by General Smith, and you know, ultimately he was responsible to General Janvier in Zagreb, but day to day, they would have been under Smith's command. Though to clarify for anybody else, Smith wasn't spending his time directing where the JCOs went. That would have been part of a much bigger strategy.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you please tell us, the Trial Chamber, who and on what grounds had command of these JSO [as interpreted] teams, because General Smith told them where to go.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, to be honest, I'm not sure what degree General Smith would have told them where to go, where not to go. They were under command of an SAS company commander who will have done most of the planning for it. No doubt plans would have been approved by General Smith, but their offices were located within the headquarters rather than within any particular battalion or national headquarters. So, yes, there was definitely a close -- a close link to the commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you used the acronym SAS, could you please explain to the Chamber what it stands for and whether they also made part of UNPROFOR and under whose command were they? Were they commanded by any UNPROFOR commander in the field, or did they have a separate commander up in the headquarters, in the command?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: SAS stands for Special Air Services -- Special Air Service, and they are British special forces. As far as command chain in-country goes, I'm vague in my memory of who was running what as far as they were concerned personally. I was nothing to do with them apart from the fact that we worked out of the same headquarters. General Smith was commander of all troops within -- within Bosnia, and therefore they would have ultimately come under his command. Generally if those troops were deployed into somebody else's area, so if, for instance, they were deployed to ground controlled by the Dutch Battalion, it would seem extremely likely that the Dutch Battalion commander had been informed that a group of these troops would be operating in his area, and there would have to be a degree of liaison concerning who covered what specific responsibilities whilst in that area. But -- sorry, but to take that forward slightly more, my only experience of actually spending time on the ground with them was in Zepa, so I'm not particularly familiar with how that command relationship operated between them and, for instance, the Dutch Battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. There was no DutchBat in Zepa, but let's take Srebrenica, for example. Did the Special Air Forces have as one of their tasks to locate targets for their air force?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that DutchBat had no aviation, then they probably would not have been in charge of those special forces. To the extent of the knowledge you have and based on your experience, could you tell us who they might have been commanded by in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. What I do remember is that the UNPROFOR was able to call upon close air support, which was provided by NATO planes rather than by UN planes. It was a fairly strange chain of command which must have been particularly frustrating for senior military officers to work with, sort of a UN and NATO chain splitting that link. However, I'm clear that the right or ability to use airpower, close air support, in times of crisis was available to all UN troops, and I believe it was one of General Smith's concerns that some units who weren't as familiar with working within the NATO chain of command may have been at a slight disadvantage to that effect. So the SAS troops work as JCOs, as far as I'm aware, and again I was listening in on the radio net. We're talking through to air operations commander, but that was in a UN headquarters building. So ultimately at the end of your question, I still believe they would have ultimately been commanded by General Smith in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that there seems to be a dual chain of command, there was one chain under NATO and the air forces on the one hand, and on the other, General Smith and UNPROFOR. How was this duality resolved in practice, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I know only, you know, the rough theory of it, not the full intricacies, but it was -- and they called it the dual key. So there would be a UN -- figuratively a UN key to turn to say, "We want close air support," and simultaneously somebody in the NATO command would have to authorise that. Now, I can't remember the ins and outs as to whether it was ultimately Janvier or whether it was Smith who turned that key. I believe later on around sort of September, Janvier was on leave, and at that stage General Smith definitely turned the key for the UN. But obviously the process did involve a degree of close liaison between NATO and the UN to ensure that these things could be effected properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To be fair to you, I just want to share with you that before you we heard testimony about -- from some people who were in command, who told us that General Janvier was against the use of aviation in Srebrenica, whereas some others were in favour of that. One would conclude that Janvier was present at the time of events in Srebrenica. Do you recall that being the case, or have you perhaps confused some things in your memory?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I think I said when Janvier was on leave was slightly later on, around sort of September time rather than Srebrenica time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he competent to make decisions on the use of aviation during the events in Srebrenica in July rather than September?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. To be completely fair to you, I wanted to ask you this: Do you know whether there was a plan to use a greater number of planes in the case of Srebrenica than the one that was actually used, and if so, why was it not implemented?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- my knowledge of these events of the use of air upon Srebrenica are fairly limited, and on Friday we discussed briefly what I'd heard on the -- on the JCO net, where one of their call-signs was calling in what was very definitely close air support. His position was being fired on by a tank. I'm aware that the air controller was saying more planes were available should they be needed, and at the time there was some dispute on the ground with the commander of the Dutch Battalion saying -- I'm saying the commander of the Dutch Battalion. Someone in the Dutch Battalion saying they didn't want more air-strikes being put in. My assumption at the time was they didn't want them put in because they were coming under pressure from the Serb side, under pressure, I mean under threat from the Serb side, being told if airpower continued, force would be used against the Dutch troops. So more planes could have been used is my belief if the decision had been taken to use them, but that particular JCO patrol had a problem with a particular tank which was silenced by the airpower. That particular team, therefore, had no further need for close air support.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you were in Srebrenica, did you inquire about the locations of the air-strikes, and did you go into the town itself? Did you see it for yourself?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember inquiring about the air-strikes themselves, and again I was very much following General Nicolai on that occasion. Yes, we were shown part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what you recall seeing in that town?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic was showing us what they wanted to show us in the town, and what I particularly remember was him taking us to one of the graveyards where he showed us some Serb headstones which he said had been defiled by the population of Srebrenica, and I now can't remember if they had been hammered or shot or whatever. So that's one of the things that does stick in my mind on that particular day. I spoke earlier about seeing the detritus left behind from the concentration of IDPs gathered within Srebrenica, and I don't remember the town being particularly badly damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the damage caused by the VRS or by the refugees who went to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't remember there being a great deal of damage. Certainly the bits that we were shown, I don't remember looking badly destroyed, so I don't there's anything to -- I'm not talking about destruction by the refugees, that's for sure. It -- it was my opinion, actually, that when we got to Zepa, it looked as though there'd actually been slightly more destruction in Zepa, and even that wasn't a huge amount when we first arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said for the record that there was quite a lot of rubbish in the UNPROFOR base, did anyone from the VRS enter the base prior to DutchBat leaving in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to clarify, the rubbish that I saw was outside the base. I believe we were standing on the road outside the Dutch Battalion headquarters. I simply don't know if anybody from the VRS went into it before the Dutch left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at -- since you moved on to Zepa, look at paragraph 5, page 2, where you refer to the arrival in Zepa with an SAS captain with the task of reporting back to General Smith about what was going on in Zepa. You say in the seventh row, in the seventh line, that you had sophisticated radio equipment at your disposal. What was the equipment to be used for, and what were you expected to do with it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one of the of most reliable radio sets that we had, a TacSat, which was what Mike Stanley, my predecessor, and I would fairly regularly carry to Pale if we were dealing with communications from headquarters there back to Sarajevo. So it wasn't unusual that our group would have that particular equipment, and as we discussed before, it was part of the eyes and ears role of what we were doing that we could use that equipment to pass information reliably and in a timely manner back to HQ UNPROFOR via the JCO office.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We might have our first break now despite of the fact that we started later today, because of another commitment. We adjourn now and resume at quarter past 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My apologies for the delay. Mr. Tolimir, please proceed with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We now arrive in Zepa in terms of our questions. Rather than going back to your statement again, can you tell us, please, who you met in Zepa, and what did those people represent? Who were they the representatives of?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we first arrived we got up to what is known as OP 2, which was on the hill above the village itself, and I believe up there we found yourself and General Mladic, and also present were the ICRC, who were talking to General Mladic at the time, trying to negotiate permission to go down in the village, which they did. We got permission to go down. There was myself, the French colonel and his interpreter, and I think the civil affairs guys came down with us. Drove down to the bottom of the hill into the village itself, where we met a number of the -- a very small number of the civilian population, and again it's 50, 80, something like that, people in town. At some stage that afternoon we met Avdo Palic, who was the commander of the BiH, the Bosnian Army. I believe there was also a civilian called Dr. Benjamin, Dr. Benjamin, who was at that stage looking after a number of sick and elderly in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us who did you arrive in Zepa with out of those representing international organisations? We'll move on to Benjamin and the rest, but can you tell us what other representatives of international organisations were there, such as UNHCR, UNPROFOR, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. There were the small British contingent, myself plus two JCOs; there were two members of UN Civil Affairs, Ed Joseph and Viktor Bezruchenko; and the ICRC I said we met. I don't recall UNHCR being present at OP 2. I don't recall them being present in Zepa at all. At some stage we ended up with a slightly larger French contingent than just the colonel and his interpreter, but again I can't remember whether they arrived with us initially or whether they came sometime after we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Those were the representatives of the international organisations that you can recall, as you said in your statement. Who was the French colonel you mentioned in the transcript, in your previous answer? What French contingent did he belong to, since we saw that the British contingent was included in JCO teams. If I'm mistaken in any way, please correct me.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. The French colonel was a legionnaire colonel from the French Foreign Legion. I'm assuming he was based out of Sector Sarajevo but I don't -- I'm fairly sure he wasn't -- he wasn't based out of BiH headquarters, as far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us his name, given that he commanded the French contingent, or was someone else in command of the French contingent present at check-point number 2 during the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- I had difficulty last time remembering his name. It wasn't Janvier. It's Jardine, something like that, Jardinier. He was the senior French officer there. He was not the commander of the French -- French troops of Sector Sarajevo in Sarajevo at all. He was just a unit commander, and in our time in Zepa he was replaced by an engineer colonel whose name I don't recall at all. And when I say "colonel," again I don't recall whether they were lieutenant-colonels or full colonels.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the task of the British contingent that you were the head of, and what was the task of the French contingent? Please explain that to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understood it, our role was, again, eyes and ears, go and see what is happening in Zepa. I believe the intention behind that was to try and ensure that the evacuation of people from Zepa ran as smoothly as possible, and again if my recollection is correct, by that stage HQ UNPROFOR was aware or certainly believed that atrocities of some sort had taken place in Srebrenica, and therefore and part of that hope was that our presence on the ground would do something to ensure that did not happen a second time, i.e., during the evacuation of Zepa. And I think that's probably backed up by the fact that General Smith himself made a number of personal visits to OP 2 but not to Zepa itself, but he made sure that as commander of UN troops in Bosnia he was seen on the ground and was dealing with General Mladic on the ground. The French -- the mission of the French contingent versus the mission of the British contingent, I think we were there for pretty much the same thing. They would have provided a same language eyes and ears interpretation to head of Sector Sarajevo. We provided an English eyes and ears to General Smith. You referred to me as the commander of the group. I'm not actually sure that's correct. There were three of us, two of us were captains. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise if I was mistaken. It seemed to me that you mentioned something along the lines of you being -- or the British continent being there with you. Perhaps I misinterpreted it, and I'd like to have that reflected in the transcript. When you arrived in Zepa, were you limited in terms of movement in Zepa, be it yourself or the British contingent or Joseph and Bezruchenko, or were you free to move about and to speak to the Bosnian civilians and the army?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the day we arrived, we were able to speak to the civilian population there. We were able to speak with Avdo Palic. As time went on, restrictions were put on us, but to answer your question strictly as to when we arrived, we had reasonable freedom of access.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the VRS restrict your movement in Zepa in any way, or were you restricted by the Bosnian Army and their authorities given that there were no Serb soldiers in Zepa itself?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but we were relatively sensible in where we thought our boundaries were. So obviously before coming down into Zepa itself we made sure we were given permission by General Mladic. It was a relatively restricted group that came down initially, and if I recall right -- well, I do recall, the two JCOs remained at the top of the hill and I travelled down with the French colonel and his interpreter. And our small group were dealing with the problem that faced us immediately within Zepa, which was the civilian population coming into the village itself, and we were not trying to, ourselves, get out and about beyond the -- the limits of Zepa village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I think perhaps my question was unclear. Did any of you who came on behalf of UNPROFOR or some international organisation have the Serbian Army restrict movement? Of course you didn't go to the combat zone because of the mines, but were you prevented from moving and being in regular contact with your HQ and other activities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not restricted at all in speaking to our HQ. That was absolutely fine. As I said before, we didn't test the boundaries as to how far we could go. The initial group let down into the village was restricted, but subsequently the rest of our team was allowed in. I do recall a day or so later some press wanted to come down and General Mladic escorted them as far as the outskirts of Zepa to where the two newish-looking cabins were, but didn't bring them all the way into the village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't ask you about journalists. We can deal with that later, but thank you for speaking about that. Anyway, can you please tell us, were you able to freely monitor the entire evacuation process? Let's first stick to this question and then we will move to journalists.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to monitor the entire evacuation that took place within Zepa village itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you notice that members of the Army of Republika Srpska were forbidden from entering Zepa for as long as the population was there, until the evacuation process was completed? Thank you. That they were forbidden from mingling with the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. They were kept out of the village centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness now, please, D107, D107. This is a presidential decree or announcement by the president of the UN Security Council, issued on the 20th of July, 1995, and this is 3556. The session is 3556 of the Security Council, and the topic of the session is Zepa. And the number of the document is D107. Thank you. We can now see it on the screen. I'm going to read just one paragraph. "The Security Council underlines the importance it attaches to the fullest co-operation with the UNHCR and other international humanitarian organisations, and demands that they be given unhindered freedom of movement and access to that area. It further demands that the Bosnian Serb authorities co-operate with all efforts, including those of UNPROFOR, to ensure the safety of the civilian population, and in particular, its most vulnerable members, including evacuation as requested by the Foreign Minister of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in his letter of the 17th of July, 1995." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Pursuant to this statement by the president of the Security Council, were you able to have contacts with the Muslim population in Zepa, and was it possible for UNPROFOR to be at OP 2 with the French contingent, and you were also able to enter with the special members of the British Army that you discussed earlier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to get into the village as discussed, and we were able to talk with the Muslim population. To clarify that, we were only able to talk with those members of the population who had come into the village, which tended to be women, some young boys, old men. But, yes, those that were there, we were able to speak to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please now tell us whether during your stay in Zepa you were able to carry out all of the activities that the Security Council urged in this statement of the 20th of July, 1995, that we referred to just now?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just read through it once again. To a large extent, yes, we were able to -- to do as was said. One incident sticks out in my mind, and that was the -- forbidding the hodja to leave Zepa as a member of the civilian population. I think to fulfil that to a hundred per cent, certainly from a personal point of view, and I know civil affairs felt the same, they believed that the hodja should have been allowed to leave Zepa as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember which hodja it was, what was his name, and did he later come out through the check-point at Boksanica, or OP 2 as you call it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I don't recall his name. He was a young-ish guy who -- clearly a civilian. He got up the hill as far as what we call OP 2 with the very final contingent of civilian population, and as he was preparing to leave, you personally said that he was not able to leave, and that was protested by the UN Civil Affairs people, but they/we lost the protest and the hodja was not allowed to leave from Zepa or from OP 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point in time were you aware that that hodja, by profession, who was not carrying out the duties of a hodja, was the president of the Zepa War Presidency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. But what I did see him doing was looking after the civilian population, which he clearly knew very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see if he was making lists, organising the evacuation, people entering, boarding buses, allocating them into buses? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was participating in that process, and at one stage towards the end, I remember him specifically saying, "There's still one old man, I think, who hasn't left the village yet," and he directed UNPROFOR to where this guy was and ensured that he was collected and evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness, please, P736, P736.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, these activities that the hodja was carrying out, do they indicate that he was an organiser and that everybody listened and obeyed to him, including civilians and UNPROFOR and so on, and he was actually carrying out the duties, as we will see, of a member of the War Presidency of the municipality of Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the direct question I would say he was respected within his community, but obviously nothing struck me as strange about that, as the hodja is someone who I would expect to have a degree of respect in the village. Also, it's probably worth noting he was perhaps the only man of that age amongst all those people there and not unnatural that he would be taking the role that he was taking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, is there any problem broadcasting this document during the testimony of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, there is not, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just want a clarification. At page 34, line 4 to 8, you state: "One instance sticks out in my mind, and that was the forbidding -- forbidding the hodja to leave Zepa as a member of the civilian population. I think to fulfil that to a hundred per cent, certainly from my personal point of view and I know civil affairs felt the same, they felt that the hodja should be allowed to leave Zepa as well." Can you explain the last one? You felt -- was this your professional conclusion or your personal view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Professional conclusion, and that was, you know, backed up by civil affairs who argued that the man should leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that feeling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was forbidden to leave by General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Why did you personally feel that he should have been allowed to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I saw him as a man who had not participated, from what I could see, in the conflict. He was a civilian looking after his civilian population and had been key to keeping them together, making sure that they could leave in an orderly manner, making sure that none of his community or his flock, for want of another word, were left behind. For those reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Could you gauge his age?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trying to remember now it's slightly difficult, but would say late 20s to mid 30s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, sir, did you know that there were two persons in Zepa who had completed the training to be hodja, one of whom performed the duties of a hodja and the other one was a civilian working in the War Presidency of Zepa? Do you perhaps know that or not? If not, I can show you a document where he's being addressed by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have a follow-up question to the question of Judge Nyambe. Sir, you told us that the hodja had to leave the bus and was not allowed to go further with the bus with the other members of the population. What happened at that point in time to the hodja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was handed over to or taken into the custody of the VRS, and beyond that I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: He was not sent back to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the day this happened, the date? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was probably be on the -- on the final and fourth day. So if we arrived on the 25th, 26th, 27th, probably the 28th. Yeah, I think that's the most -- most likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the evacuation still going on on the 28th or was it finished, as you said in your statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that was the final day. So we had roughly 20 trucks on the first day, quite a good -- good session of trucks on the second day. We called for more trucks early on the third day, which had left about 400 people. We didn't quite get enough trucks to move that full 400 at the beginning of the last day, and I think I spoke to you again to get additional vehicles, which you provided. And so this was the very last day of the evacuation. What we did find when we got up to OP 2 from Zepa itself was that the buses that had left earlier that morning were still being held at OP 2. My guess being that everyone would then leave as one big party of buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you. It's hard to remember after so much time. I would like you to look at the document in e-court now. I would like you to look at these names of the War Presidency of the municipality of Zepa. You can look at it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up the English document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is a decision signed by this War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 in the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you can see where it is written "Mehmed Hajric." He was the president of the War Presidency. That is that hodja that you're talking about. Hamdija Torlak, and Amir Imamovic, and they signed. You can see their signatures. You can see the signature of General Mladic and the signature of Rajko Kusic, and this is the decision of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to the contents on the first page so that the witness can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the first paragraph where says: "The War Presidency of the Zepa municipality at its meeting held on the 27th of July, 1995, attended by Mehmed Hajric," that is the hodja that you're talking about, "president of the War Presidency, Hamdija Torlak, President of the Executive Board, and Amir Imamovic, commander of the Civilian Protection Staff, hereby adopts the following decision." And they reached the decision that all able-bodied men who happened to be in Zepa should be disarmed and they should surrender to the base in Zepa. So these signatures attest to the fact that the members of the Presidency took -- went to the Boksanica check-point and that he was driven there by members of the Ukrainian Battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure if he completely understood what Mr. Tolimir said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The witness said -- and I'm helping you if you didn't know that. Did you know that there was a witness here who signed what -- this document, who testified that the hodja took this decision to the soldiers, indicating that the decision had been implemented?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just clarify exactly what I'm being asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you if you know that the hodja, as a member of the War Presidency, signed this decision, and then on the 27th took it to the Zepa mountain, to the soldiers, for them to act pursuant to his decision because he was a member of the War Presidency. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is the first time that I've seen anything to that effect that I recall. He may have signed it. I guess there's a degree of question as to what options were open to anybody, and I've no idea whether it was signed willingly or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If someone signs a document on behalf of the War Presidency, does that person have the authority over the able-bodied persons also? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. I don't actually know what the role of the War Presidency was. Was it simply the name given to the normal municipality in Zepa in times of war or did it actually have any control over military men of fighting age. That's simply not something I know about within the structure of whether they fit it under the armija or whether it was a purely civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document D54.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then you will know more clearly who he was and from whom he received his orders. And now we can see the document in the Serbian language on the left-hand side. Now we're going to see it in the English. And I would like you to look at the actual heading of the document where it says "Mehmed Effendi Hajric, President of Zepa - protected." Does this title in the heading, the Effendi, indicate that he was a member of the clergy?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it might, but I'm not -- I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you look at the bottom left-hand corner of the document, both in the English and the B/C/S, it says that this document is sent from Sarajevo on the 19th of July, 1995, by Alija Izetbegovic. Do you see that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see Alija Izetbegovic's name in the signature block, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that Alija Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and at the same time he was the president of the Crisis Staff of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew he was president of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did I know he was president of the crisis council? I'm not sure. It certainly doesn't surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that each municipality in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in wartime, which was under the control of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had a War Presidency of the municipality that was connected to the president of the state, Alija Izetbegovic, and that the duty of the War Presidency was being carried out by Alija Izetbegovic who in this case is addressing Mehmed Effendi Hajric, who was the president of the Zepa War Presidency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall being aware that everywhere had a War Presidency, but again I don't recall not being aware of that. And it seems -- thinking about it, it seems logical that in a time of crisis there would be some form of council, things -- even municipal matters would no doubt be managed in a slightly different line from how they are in peacetime. That makes -- that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We're now going to look at paragraph 2 so that you can see that he was addressing him in terms -- in relation to the job that you were monitoring in Zepa and it states: "An evacuation is possible only by land under the supervision of UNPROFOR. I am in contact with General Smith every day. The Chetniks are dragging out the talks on purpose. General Smith is guaranteeing the security of women and children. You know that there is no fool-proof security. As their first condition, the Chetniks have asked that the men lay down their weapons and their investigation and so on, which I refused categorically for reasons I do not need to explain to you." Thank you. And we can also look at paragraph 3, the first sentence: "My plan: Move out as many civilians as possible, all if possible." As you can see, this was written on the 19th of July, and he's addressing him about what civilians need to do because he was the president of the municipal War Presidency. And then the next sentence in paragraph 3 states: "We will do all to help you by supplying materiel and equipment, volunteers, and offensive action in your direction ..." Based on this, is it clear from this second sentence in paragraph 3 that Alija Izetbegovic was writing to him also about military activities, what the army was going to do, what the volunteers were going to do, how he would provide equipment and materiel to him and how this would assist in the combat activities? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that's covered in the letter, but again nothing strikes me as unusual. If somebody is being briefed on the situation in his area, if he is a senior civilian administrator in an area that's about to be captured or has been captured, it would be indeed correct that he should be briefed as to the entire set of circumstances happening around him, including his own, the disposition of Bosnian Army forces. And I'm also very clear in my own mind that this particular man wanted to leave Zepa, and it was, you know, his intention to leave as part of the civilian population. And I'm seeing this document for the first time, but there's talk of continuing along your own roads in your own way. This particular man had no intention of staying on in Zepa. His intention was to get on the bus or the truck and leave Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the last sentence of paragraph 3, which states: "Would you please let me know which plan to push?" Why would hodja need to report back to Alija Izetbegovic about which plan to push if he wasn't in some kind of post and if his intention was to leave Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm reading the English translation, and I can't see where it says that he needs to ask or report back as to which roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just above item 4. It begins with "Let me." Do you see that? And perhaps you can check the versions in both languages since you speak both of them.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All right. I didn't read far enough down. Let me just read the middle of it. And let me just read your question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'll repeat. Why is Alija Izetbegovic requesting of him to let him know which plan to push if he was a mere hodja? He had no other functions or duties to perform.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. You're asking me to speculate way beyond what I know, but accepting that I'm speculating, we're talking about a joint withdrawal which could be a joint withdrawal of the civilian population through wooded areas back to Bosnian-held territory, and as that's a move that involves the civilian population for which he is a representative, it's conceivable, certainly, that that is what he was going to inform about. It certainly doesn't have to have a purely military connotation by -- according to my reading of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at the second sentence of paragraph 3, where it says: "We will do everything to help you by supplying MTS, volunteers, and to launch offensive action in your direction ..." Does this refer to military activities?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would assume so, but again it's informing him of the situation as a whole. The civilian population is cut off. I don't see what's particularly unusual that he should be saying, "We," as in Sarajevo government, "are doing everything to assist you and your population cut off in Zepa." That's entirely reasonable in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you and your answer. Please have a look at D51 next.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Serbian we see the text of an agreement on the disarmament of able-bodied men in the enclave of Zepa containing ten items. It was signed by a certain Hamdija Torlak as well as Rajko Kusic and Ratko Mladic. We saw a moment ago a decision on the disarmament of able-bodied men signed by Hajric. This document was produced on the 24th. The decision we just saw signed by Hajric was dated the 27th. Do you believe that he had anything to do with the disarmament of able-bodied men in the enclave of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, do I believe that the hodja had anything to do with the disarmament of able-bodied men? I personally didn't witness any disarmament of able-bodied men so it's difficult to say, but I saw nothing to suggest that he had been disarming anybody. I'm not actually aware that any able-bodied men were disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at the title. It says "Agreement on the disarmament of the able-bodied population in the Zepa enclave." Have I quoted correctly?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was this agreement signed? If you can check the first sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date in the first line is the 24 July, so the day before I got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it say that on that day the following agreement was reached between the person referred to specifically? Is that the first sentence of the document?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB [Resumed]
